newsitem.title: USA: Fed must seek effective zero inflation - Melzer.
newsitem.headline: Fed must seek effective zero inflation - Melzer.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's goal should be to attain and maintain an effective zero rate of U.S. inflation, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis President Thomas Melzer said on Thursday.

"There is so much debate about the zigs and zags of monetary policy that sometimes the big picture falls out of focus," Melzer told the St. Louis Society of Financial Analysts in an address that was made available in New York.
"The aim is to move inflation toward an effective rate of zero and keep it there," he said.
Melzer said one problem with U.S. monetary policy is the absence of a target that would enhance the Fed's credibility regarding achieving price stability.

"While Fed officials sometimes discuss stable prices as a long-term goal, the Federal Open Market Committee has not identified a price index that provides a reliable measure of inflation, nor has it specified a target range that would be acceptable," he said.
New York Fed President William McDonough commented on the same topic -- a target for Fed policy -- in a speech before the Economic Club of New York late on Wednesday.

"Price stability should be the sole long-run objective of monetary policy," Melzer said. "Adopting this stance would put all policymakers as well as the public, Congress and financial market participants on the same page with respect to Fed objectives."
He said one big advantage of adopting a target would be that the Fed could change rates "without creating consternation in financial markets about its resolve to keep inflation low."
"The FOMC should announce its inflation forecasts a number of years into the future," he added.
"An organized, well-publicized and fully expected policy move toward a stable price environment should pose no danger to the real economy," Melzer added.
He stressed the dangers of not meeting a price-stability goal.
"Failure to make a firm commitment to price stability puts upward pressure on the inflation-risk premium in interest rates," he said.
He also said the issuance of inflation-indexed bonds would not fully erase inflation expectations priced into market rates.
"Indexed-linked debt, as it is being proposed by the Treasury, is not a perfect solution to the elimination of the inflation-risk premium in interest rates," Melzer said.
But he acknowledged that "index-linked debt reduces the incentive for fiscal authorities to pressure the central bank to monetize the government debt."
He stressed that inflation-indexed instruments cannot, by themselves, erase inflation.

"The government can save financing costs if the Fed is able to deliver a better inflation performance than the financial markets expect," Melzer said. "I hope the Fed will actually deliver, over time, the lower-than-expected inflation necessary for this to occur."
